# Introduction

There are number of sources of crop production data. The three main sources identified for Nigeria have different dates, and differing number of crops ( @tbl-Sources ).

+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-------------------+-----------------+
| Source       | Spatial Resolution | Most recent data | Crops             | Indicators      |
+==============+====================+=================:+===================+=================+
| NAERLS/FMAFS | State              | 2024             | - Banana/Plantain | - Area          |
|              |                    |                  | - Cassava         | - Production    |
|              |                    |                  | - Cowpea          | - Yield         |
|              |                    |                  | - Maize           |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Rice            |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Sorghum         |                 |
+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-------------------+-----------------+
| HarvestStat  | State              | 2006-2023        | - Banana          | - Cropped Area  |
|              |                    |                  | - Cassava         | - Production    |
|              |                    |                  | - Cowpea          | - Yield         |
|              |                    |                  | - Maize           |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Rice            |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Sorghum         |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Sweet Potato    |                 |
+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-------------------+-----------------+
| MapSpam      | 5' Pixel           | 2020             | - Banana/Plantain | - Physical Area |
|              |                    |                  | - Cassava         | - Harvest Area  |
|              |                    |                  | - Cowpea          | - Production    |
|              |                    |                  | - Maize           | - Yield         |
|              |                    |                  | - Rice            |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Sorghum         |                 |
|              |                    |                  | - Sweet Potato    |                 |
+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-------------------+-----------------+
| WorldCover   | 10m                | 2021
: Crop Production data sources for Nigeria {#tbl-Sources}

# Methods

The data at state level need to be joined to the Nigeria States spatial dataset.

The stages are:

1.  Load the States dataset
2.  Load each crop database
3.  For each crop in the database join to the state spatial dataset and plot

## Load the States

The source of the states data is from OSGOF-Ehealth-UNCS.
These have previously been cleaned to remove sliver polygons and gaps, and were saved as a topojson format.

```{r}
#| label: states
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| results: asis

vect_state_geo <- vect("D:/DatosProyecto/SpatialData/Africa/Pais/Nigeria/NGA Admin 2019-2025 OSGOF-Ehealth-UNCS/nga_admin1_topo.topojson")

crs(vect_state_geo) <- "epsg:4326"

vect_state_geo$adm1_pcode <- as.factor(vect_state_geo$adm1_pcode)

# levels(vect_state_geo$adm1_pcode) # Check levels

ggplot(vect_state_geo)+
  geom_spatvector(aes(fill = adm1_pcode)) +
  geom_spatvector_text(aes(label = adm1_pcode), size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria States",
    fill = "State<br>Code") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_markdown(),
    legend.title = element_markdown(),
    axis.title = element_blank()
  )

df_state <- as.data.frame(vect_state_geo)


```

## NAERLS/FMAFS crop database

The NAERLS/FMAFS crop database [@naerls/fmafs2024WetSeason2024] has csv files for each crop. The csv files need to be loaded and joined to the state dataset.

**Banana/Plantain** data are loaded and are available for the following states:

```{r}
#| label: naerls_plantain_banana
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| results: asis

df_naerls_plantain_banana <- read.csv("D:/DatosProyecto/SpatialData/Africa/Pais/Nigeria/NAERLS Crop Stats 2024/Plantain_Banana.csv")
df_naerls_plantain_banana$State <- as.factor(df_naerls_plantain_banana$State)
cat(paste(levels(df_naerls_plantain_banana$State), "; ")) # Check levels

vect_plantain_banana_2024 <- dplyr::left_join(vect_state_geo, df_naerls_plantain_banana, by = c("adm1_name" = "State"))

df_plantain_banana_2024 <- as.data.frame(vect_plantain_banana_2024) |> rename(plantain_banana_2024 = Area_Ha_2024)

```

## NASS crop database

The Nigerian National Bureau of Statistics 2022 National Agricultural Sample Survey (NASS) crop database [] has an excel sheet that has been converted to csv files for each crop. 
The survey collected data from two seasons - the major season and the minor season. The minor season is in general the dry season in the north of the country, with crops grown under irrigation or residual moisture. In the south the minor season may also be dry but could be also be the minor rainy season in the second half of the year.

The csv files need to be loaded and joined to the state dataset.

**Banana/Plantain** data are loaded and are available for the following states:

```{r}
#| label: nass_plantain_banana
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| results: asis

df_nass_plantain_banana <- read.csv("E:/repos/Nigeria_Biofortification_Atlas/tab_data/NASS_Crop_Stats_2022_23/Plantain_Banana_NASS.csv")
df_nass_plantain_banana$State <- as.factor(df_nass_plantain_banana$State)
cat(paste(levels(df_nass_plantain_banana$State), "; ")) # Check levels

# replace NA with 0
df_nass_plantain_banana[][df_nass_plantain_banana[] == "#DIV/0!"] <- 0
df_nass_plantain_banana[][df_nass_plantain_banana[] == NA] <- 0

vect_plantain_banana_2022 <- dplyr::left_join(vect_state_geo, df_nass_plantain_banana, by = c("adm1_name" = "State"))

df_plantain_banana_2022 <- as.data.frame(vect_plantain_banana_2022) |> rename(plantain_banana_2022 = h_area_22_23_T)

```

## MapSpam 2020 

The MapSpam 2020 [@youGeneratingGlobalCrop2014] data are provided as GeoTiff raster images.

::: callout-note
### Total area per grid cell

The spatial resolution of each cell in MapSpam 2020 is 5 arc minutes. This means that there is not a constant total area, but we can estimate the total area per cell for Nigeria:

Latitude side (5 arc-minutes north-south): 1° of latitude ≈ 111.2 km (nearly constant everywhere on Earth) 5' = 5/60° → 111.2 × (5/60) ≈ 9.27 km

Longitude side (5 arc-minutes east-west): 1° of longitude shrinks with latitude by a factor of cos(latitude). At 10°N: cos(10°) ≈ 0.9848 1° longitude ≈ 111.2 × 0.9848 ≈ 109.5 km 5' = 109.5 × (5/60) ≈ 9.13 km

Area of the grid cell: 9.27 km × 9.13 km ≈ 84.6 km²

Convert to hectares (1 km² = 100 ha): 84.6 × 100 ≈ 8,460 hectares

This means that no cell has more than 10,000 hectares, this knowledge is useful for plotting the crops.
:::

## MapSpam 2020 - Total area per state 

In order to produce maps of crop production at the state level there are two methods. The first method is to calculate the zonal statistics of the crop raster datasets, within the state polygons. The second method is to load the MapSpam csv files which already have codes for each state. The csv file uses the centroid location of the raster. In some cases the centroid appears to be in a different state to that which appears in the csv table, but the MapSpam data use crop statistics as part of the model, so it is safer to assume that the state name is correct.

# Compare data sources

To help select the best data source it is necessary to compare the state statistics for each crop from the three sources.


## Total crop area

### NAERLS/FMAFS crop database

Add the harvested area for each crop and sum to obtain an estimate of the total crop area.
I parsed all 17 crop tables in Section 12.0 (Rice, Maize, Sorghum, Millet, Cowpea, Groundnut, Soybean, Benniseed, Yam, Cassava, Cocoyam, Cotton, Ginger, Tomato, Onion, Okra, Plantain/Banana) and summed the "Land Area (Ha)" figures for each state across all crops it grows. The state-level sums total almost exactly to the sum of the national totals given in each table (a good cross-check), confirming the extraction is accurate.

Not every state grows every crop, so each state's total reflects however many of the 17 crops were reported for it (ranging from 7 crops for Rivers up to 15 for Benue, Taraba, and Plateau).
FCT and Bauchi top the list, largely driven by very large reported areas under crops like yam and cassava (whose land-area figures are much bigger than cereals per state).

Zamfara, Sokoto, and Katsina show the largest declines in total cropped area in 2024 vs 2023.

In addition to crops not reported these are the report's own land-area estimates per crop (Table 12.1–12.17), not an independent GIS measurement — some of the same land may be double-cropped or intercropped, so this "total area" is a sum of reported cultivated hectares per crop rather than a literal footprint of unique land.

**Total Cropped Area** data are loaded and are available for the following states:

```{r}
#| label: naerls_total_cropped
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| results: asis

df_naerls_total_cropped <- read.csv("E:/repos/Nigeria_Biofortification_Atlas/tab_data/NAERLS_Crop_Stats_2024/nigeria_crop_area_by_state_2023_24.csv")

# change name to match states dataset
df_naerls_total_cropped['State'][df_naerls_total_cropped['State'] == "FCT"] <- "Federal Capital Territory"


df_naerls_total_cropped$State <- as.factor(df_naerls_total_cropped$State)
cat(paste(levels(df_naerls_total_cropped$State), "; ")) # Check levels

vect_total_cropped_2024 <- dplyr::left_join(vect_state_geo, df_naerls_total_cropped, by = c("adm1_name" = "State"))

df_total_cropped_2024 <- as.data.frame(vect_total_cropped_2024)

```

```{r}
#| label: naerls_total_cropped_map_2024
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
#| results: asis

ggplot(vect_total_cropped_2024) +
  geom_spatvector(aes(fill = Area_Ha_2024)) +
  geom_spatvector_text(aes(label = adm1_pcode), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_stepsn(
```

### WorldCover 30

The WorldCover dataset has a spatial resolution of 10m, and includes a landcover class for cropland [@zanagaESAWorldCover102022]. 
The original raster needs to be reclassified as 1 for cropland and 0 for all other classes.
Zonal statistics are then computed for each state - giving a pixel count. This value needs to be divided by 100 to give a value in hectares.

### Compare sources for total crop area

The table below displays all four sources together. The data are initially sorted according to the NAERLS data source, and by default the table shows the top 15 states - but you can change the number displayed. You can also change which column to sort by clicking on the arrows, and search for a specific state.


```{r}
#| label: compare_sources_total
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true


df_total_comb <- dplyr::left_join(
  dplyr::select(
    df_total_cropped_2024,
    adm1_pcode,
    adm1_ref_name,
    Area_Ha_2024,
    Area_Ha_2023
  ),
  dplyr::select(df_wc_nigeria_crop, NAME_1, Area_Ha_2021),
  by = c('adm1_ref_name' = "NAME_1")
) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(df_nass_total_cropped, adm1_ref_name, sum_area),
    by = 'adm1_ref_name'
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(df_spam_total, by = c('adm1_ref_name' = 'ADM1_NAME'))


df_total_comb_rename <- df_total_comb |> dplyr::rename(NAERLS_2024 = Area_Ha_2024, NAERLS_2023 = Area_Ha_2023, NASS_2022 = sum_area, WC_2021 = Area_Ha_2021, MapSpam_2020 = total)

df_total_comb_rename_round <- df_total_comb_rename

df_total_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024 <- round(df_total_comb_rename$NAERLS_2024, digits = 0)
df_total_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2023 <- round(df_total_comb_rename$NAERLS_2023, digits = 0)
df_total_comb_rename_round$NASS_2022 <- round(df_total_comb_rename$NASS_2022, digits = 0)
df_total_comb_rename_round$WC_2021 <- round(df_total_comb_rename$WC_2021, digits = 0)
df_total_comb_rename_round$MapSpam_2020 <- round(df_total_comb_rename$MapSpam_2020, digits = 0)


df_total_comb_rename_round |>
  base::sort_by(df_total_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024, decreasing = T) |>
  DT::datatable(
    rownames = F,
    filter = "bottom",
    selection = list(mode = "none"),
    editable = FALSE,
    options = list(
      digits = 0,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      scrollCollapse = TRUE,
      autoWidth = TRUE,
      fixedColumns = list(leftColumns = 2),
      lengthMenu = c(15, 40),
      pageLength = 15
    )
  )

```


<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>


The comparison of crop areas among the sources shows some very large discrepancies among the sources. The most obvious difference is for the Federal Capital Territory. The NAERLS source gives a total crop area in excess of 2 million hectares, this in spite of the fact that the actual total area of the FCT (including urban areas, grassland, woodland etc.) is less than a million hectares.

Because NAERLS compiles its report using data sent in from individual State Agricultural Development Programmes (ADPs) and Ministries of Agriculture, errors usually trace back to a few specific systematic systemic issues: 

- The Double-Counting Trap: If a single field in the FCT was used to grow multiple crops simultaneously (intercropping, such as mixing maize, sorghum, and cowpeas on the same plot), the data collectors likely recorded the full size of that field for each individual crop. When those crop areas were summed together vertically, it generated an inflated "total crop area" that exceeded the physical size of the land.
- Data Entry and Decimal Errors: A misplaced comma, extra zero, or basic typo during data aggregation can instantly turn a minor regional figure into a national peak.
- Flawed Projection Baselines: Lacking a real-time satellite mapping infrastructure, local agencies often rely on rough estimates or outdated population multipliers to guess cultivated areas, which completely breaks down when applied to a rapidly developing urban territory like FCT.

The NASS gives very large harvested areas for northern states like Kano Bauchi and Niger states. The data are derived from a household survey, so it is possible that there is double-counting where crops are grown together, or that plot areas are not calculated precisely.

The Worldcover map, in contrast, gives extremely low cropland cover estimates for the southern states. This may be because the classification algorithm doesn't discriminate well between bushy semi-perennial crops - like cassava, or plantain - and shrub or tree cover, or because the cloud cover did not allow for sufficient satellite imagery.

```{r}
  DT::datatable(

```

<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

The NAERLS/FMAFS and HarvestStat data are more or less consistent, and it is likely that the HarvestStat data are the same as the NAERLS/FMAFS data from 2021.
However, there are significant differences with the NASS data from 2022-23 and the MapSpam data for 2020. MapSpam has banana and plantain data for many more states than the other two sources. The patterns are different however: Kwara is the state with the largest area of banana and plantain in the NAERLS and HarvestStat sources, but has no harvested area in the MapSpam 2020 data.

The NASS data do not give values for individual states in the three northern geopolitical zones. The North Central zone has a harvested area of approximately 50,000ha of banana and plantain, but it is difficult to assign the area to states.

As a consequence, and despite the inconsistencies, the most suitable data to use are the NAERLS/FMAFS data from 2024 for Banana and Plantain due to the recency of the data.

### Compare sources

The table below displays all four sources together. The data are initially sorted according to the NAERLS data source, and  by default the table shows the top 15 states - but you can change the number displayed. You can also change which column to sort by clicking on the arrows, and search for a specific state.


```{r}
#| label: compare_sources_cass
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true


df_cass_comb <- dplyr::left_join(
  dplyr::select(
    df_cassava_2024,
    adm1_pcode,
    adm1_ref_name,
    cassava_2024
  ),
  dplyr::select(df_cassava_2023, adm1_pcode, cassava_2023),
  by = 'adm1_pcode'
) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(df_cassava_2022, cassava_2022, adm1_ref_name),
    by = 'adm1_ref_name'
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    df_spam_cassava_2,
    by = c('adm1_ref_name' = 'ADM1_NAME')
  )


df_cass_comb_rename <- df_cass_comb |> dplyr::rename(NAERLS_2024 = cassava_2024, HarvestStat_2023 = cassava_2023, NASS_2022 = cassava_2022, MapSpam_2020 = sum_cassava)

df_cass_comb_rename_round <- df_cass_comb_rename

df_cass_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024 <- round(df_cass_comb_rename$NAERLS_2024, digits = 0)
df_cass_comb_rename_round$HarvestStat_2023 <- round(df_cass_comb_rename$HarvestStat_2023, digits = 0)
df_cass_comb_rename_round$NASS_2022 <- round(df_cass_comb_rename$NASS_2022, digits = 0)
df_cass_comb_rename_round$MapSpam_2020 <- round(df_cass_comb_rename$MapSpam_2020, digits = 0)

df_cass_comb_rename_round |>
  base::sort_by(df_cass_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024, decreasing = T) |>
  DT::datatable(
    rownames = F,
    filter = "bottom",
    selection = list(mode = "none"),
    editable = FALSE,
    options = list(
      digits = 0,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      scrollCollapse = TRUE,
      autoWidth = TRUE,
      fixedColumns = list(leftColumns = 2),
      lengthMenu = c(15, 40),
      pageLength = 15
    )
  )

```


<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

The HarvestStat appears to use the same data source as NAERLS, so these data sources are consistent. There are some notable differences with the NASS data from 2022-23 and the MapSpam data for 2020. The Federal Capital Territory has a very low harvested area in MapSpam compared with NAERLS 2024 data, and an intermediate harvested area in the NASS dataset. Similarly Bayelsa and Kwara have lower areas in MapSpam and NASS. Meanwhile in MapSpam Borno state has a very large cassava harvested area - bigger than any other state in fact. In the NAERLS source there are no data for Borno, Kano or Adamawa. The former two states are generally not considered large producers of Cassava, but Adamawa is considered a minor producing region so this omission is surprising.

The state with the largest harvested area in the NASS data is Benue, followed closely by Oyo. These are large agricultural states and the figures seem more probable than the large area given by NAERLS for Ebonyi, which has a smaller overall land area.

The NASS data is the most appropriate to use, given its provenance and despite the fact that it is two years older than the NAERLS data.

```{r}
  ) |>

    by = c('adm1_ref_name' = 'ADM1_NAME')
  )


df_cowp_comb_rename <- df_cowp_comb |> dplyr::rename(NAERLS_2024 = cowpea_2024, HarvestStat_2023 = cowpea_2023, NASS_2022 = cowpea_2022, MapSpam_2020 = sum_cowpea)

df_cowp_comb_rename_round <- df_cowp_comb_rename

df_cowp_comb_rename_round$HarvestStat_2023 <- round(df_cowp_comb_rename$HarvestStat_2023, digits = 0)
df_cass_comb_rename_round$NASS_2022 <- round(df_cowp_comb_rename$NASS_2022, digits = 0)
df_cowp_comb_rename_round$MapSpam_2020 <- round(df_cowp_comb_rename$MapSpam_2020, digits = 0)

df_cowp_comb_rename_round |>
  base::sort_by(df_cowp_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024, decreasing = T) |>
  DT::datatable(
    rownames = F,
    filter = "bottom",
    selection = list(mode = "none"),
    editable = FALSE,
    options = list(
      digits = 0,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      scrollCollapse = TRUE,
      autoWidth = TRUE,
      fixedColumns = list(leftColumns = 2),
      lengthMenu = c(15, 40),
      pageLength = 15
    )
  )

```


<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

There are some considerable differences between the NAERLS, NASS and MapSpam data. These are unlikely to be due to the 4 years difference between the sources.
The state with the largest area of cowpea in the NAERLS source is Kogi, whereas for NASS it is Kano and for MapSpam it is Zamfara. All three states have agro-ecological conditions suitable for growing cowpea, but the figures for Zamfara seem excessive - almost double the area of cowpea in Taraba - the state with the second highest harvested area. 
NAERLS acknowledge that production in Zamfara had declined recently due to adverse weather conditions, pest infestations, and reduced input use.

Other notable differences are Osun (where NAERLS estimates almost 200 thousand and MapSpam just 5544 hectares), Niger state where NASS estimates almost half a million hectares whereas the NAERLS estimates are just 80,000, and Abia where MapSpam is extremely low.

The NASS data do not give values for individual states in the three southern geopolitical zones. The South west zone has a harvested area of approximately 55,000ha of cowpea, but it is difficult to assign the area to states. Nevertheless the harvested areas are very small compared to the northern zones.

Despite the lack of data for southern zones the NASS data better capture the cowpea growing areas and do not have obvious anomalies. However, the comparison shows that year-to-year variations will have an impact on how the crop area are used and interpreted.

<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

The comparison of maize crop area between MapSpam and NAERLS show more consistency than other crops - at least for states like Gombe, Bauchi, Kaduna and Borno. A state that has a large difference is Yobe. In the 2020 MapSpam data the harvested area is less than 150,000 hectares, whereas in the NAERLS and HarvestStat data for 2024 and 2023 respectively the area is more than double. The opposite situation is encountered for Borno, although declines in production were acknowledged in the NAERLS 2024 report.

There are very big differences between NASS and the other two sources. The overall harvest area for maize is large, with five states estimated to have harvested over a million hectares each. Nevertheless, the pattern of production is more consistent with the agro-ecological zones of Nigeria. For this reason the NASS data are the best source for maize.

You can also change which column to sort by clicking on the arrows, and search for a specific state.

```{r}
#| label: compare_sources_rice
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true


df_rice_comb <- dplyr::left_join(
  dplyr::select(
    df_rice_2024,
    adm1_pcode,
    adm1_ref_name,
    rice_2024
  ),
  dplyr::select(df_rice_2023, adm1_pcode, rice_2023),
  by = 'adm1_pcode'
) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(df_rice_2022, rice_2022, adm1_ref_name),
    by = 'adm1_ref_name'
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    df_spam_rice_2,
    by = c('adm1_ref_name' = 'ADM1_NAME')
  )


df_rice_comb_rename <- df_rice_comb |> dplyr::rename(NAERLS_2024 = rice_2024, HarvestStat_2023 = rice_2023, NASS_2022 = rice_2022, MapSpam_2020 = sum_rice)

df_rice_comb_rename_round <- df_rice_comb_rename

df_rice_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024 <- round(df_rice_comb_rename$NAERLS_2024, digits = 0)
df_rice_comb_rename_round$HarvestStat_2023 <- round(df_rice_comb_rename$HarvestStat_2023, digits = 0)
df_rice_comb_rename_round$NASS_2022 <- round(df_rice_comb_rename$NASS_2022, digits = 0)
df_rice_comb_rename_round$MapSpam_2020 <- round(df_rice_comb_rename$MapSpam_2020, digits = 0)

df_rice_comb_rename_round |>
  base::sort_by(df_rice_comb_rename_round$NAERLS_2024, decreasing = T) |>
  DT::datatable(
    rownames = F,
    filter = "bottom",
    selection = list(mode = "none"),
    editable = FALSE,
    options = list(
      digits = 0,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      scrollCollapse = TRUE,
      autoWidth = TRUE,
      fixedColumns = list(leftColumns = 2),
      lengthMenu = c(15, 40),
      pageLength = 15
    )
  )

```


<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

For rice harvested area there is a strong alignment among between NAERLS and MapSpam, with Kogi, Niger and Benue states consistently high. However, there are obvious anomalies between NASS and the other sources, and a noticeably different pattern. The overall harvest areas are far higher for NASS than NAERLS, for instance, with Kano state estimated to have a harvest areas of over 1 million hectares. Kano was not a traditional rice producing state but has recently been gaining in recognition and has received investment in production and processing.

However, given the more recent data from NAERLS we will use this source for rice.

```{r}
df_sorghum_comb_rename_round$HarvestStat_2023 <- round(df_sorghum_comb_rename$HarvestStat_2023, digits = 0)
```

<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

For sorghum there are some big differences in the harvested area by state between the NAERLS and MapSpam sources. While Kano is the biggest producer in both datasets the difference between Kano and other states is extreme in the MapSpam data, with almost double the area of the next state Kaduna. Other anomalies are Niger and Edo states which have a far higher level of area in MapSpam than the other sources.

NAERLS provides no estimates for many southern states. There is likely to be some production here, perhaps for fodder rather than grain, but these estimates do not appear in the report.

Once again the overall harvested areas in the 2022 NASS source are far larger than in NAERLS. The state with the greatest harvested area is Bauchi, with over one million hectares - far in excess of the values in the NAERLS dataset. In contrast the values for Borno state are far lower.

Given the more recent data from NAERLS we will use this source for sorghum.

<div style="margin-bottom:50px;">
</div>

The comparison between the 2006 estimates from HarvestStat and those of 2020 from MapSpam show very large differences in the absolute harvested areas, with many states in the 2020 dataset showing areas an order of magnitude different, such as Niger, Benue and Taraba, or more extremely for Enugu.

The 2022 data from NASS and are far higher than NAERLS, and are more consistent with MapSpam, but there are inconsistencies. 

Sweet Potato production has increased in Nigeria, and the 2006 data are now very old. While the MapSpam data show unusual patterns and obvious missing data for Bayelsa, Ebonyi, Ekiti and Nasarawa. The MapSpam data are more recent than the 2006 data, but given the more recent data in NASS those data will be used for Sweet Potato.


# Conclusions

It is therefore necessary to use a mixture of the sources, with government sources and more recent data given a higher priority ( @tbl-Conclusion ).

+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------+
| Source       | Spatial Resolution | Most recent data | Crops (selected)      | Indicators      |
+==============+====================+=================:+=======================+=================+
| NAERLS/FMAFS | State              | 2024             | - **Banana/Plantain** | - Area          |
|              |                    |                  | - **Rice**            | - Production    |
|              |                    |                  | - **Sorghum**         | - Yield         |
+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------+
| NBS/NASS     | State              | 2022             | - **Cassava**         | - Harvest Area  |
|              |                    |                  | - **Cowpea**          | - Production    |
|              |                    |                  | - **Maize**           | - Yield         |
|              |                    |                  | - **Sweet Potato**    |                 |
+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------+
| MapSpam      | 5' Pixel           | 2020             |                       | - Harvest Area  |
|              |                    |                  |                       | - Production    |
|              |                    |                  |                       | - Yield         |
+--------------+--------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------+

: Selected Crop Production data sources for Nigeria {#tbl-Conclusion}

```{r}
df_crop_share_2024 <- df_crop_share_2024 |>
  mutate(plantain_banana_share_2024 = (plantain_banana_Area_2024/Area_Ha_2024) * 100,
         cassava_share_2024 = (cassava_Area_2024/Area_Ha_2024) * 100, 
         cowpea_share_2024 = (cowpea_Area_2024/Area_Ha_2024) * 100,

         rice_share_2024 = (rice_Area_2024/Area_Ha_2024) * 100, 
         sorghum_share_2024 = (sorghum_Area_2024/Area_Ha_2024) * 100, 
         spot_share_2020 = (spot_Area_2020/Area_Ha_2020) * 100)

vect_crop_area_share <- dplyr::left_join(vect_state_geo, df_crop_share_2024 , by = c("adm1_ref_name"))
```

# Per-capita area harvested

We use the same population data for all crops (regardless of the date of the crop harvested area). For our purposes we are most interested in the differences among geographic units rather than between crops.

We decided to use our extrapolation of population from the NBS figures to 2025.

## 2025 and 2030 state population estimates

```{r}
#| label: pop_2025
#| message: false
#| warning: false


df_pop_nbs <- read.csv("tab_data/nigeria_state_population_weights_2025_2030_csv.csv")
vect_state_geo_nbs <- tidyterra::left_join(vect_state_geo, df_pop_nbs, by = c( "adm1_ref_name" = "state_name"))

```

## Total Population - Extrapolated from NBS 2016

```{r}
#| label: fig-population_states_nbs_2025
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: false
#| results: asis
#| fig-cap: "NBS 2025 estimates of population per state"
# 

ggplot() +
  geom_spatvector(data = vect_state_geo_nbs, aes(fill = pop_est_2025), colour = "grey") +
  scale_fill_distiller(
        type = "seq",
        palette = "Blues",
        direction = 1,
        limits = c(0, 25000000),
        labels = label_comma(),
        guide = "legend"
      ) +
  labs(title = "Population per state (2025 estimate)", fill = "Persons") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_markdown(),
    legend.title = element_markdown(),
    axis.title = element_blank()
  )

```
```{r}
#| label: combine_crop_area_per_capita
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: true

df_crop_per_capita_2024_pc <- left_join(df_crop_share_2024, select(df_pop_nbs, state_name, pop_est_2025 ), by = c("adm1_ref_name" = "state_name"))

df_crop_per_capita_2024_pc <- df_crop_per_capita_2024_pc |>
  mutate(plantain_banana_pc_2024 = (plantain_banana_Area_2024/pop_est_2025) * 10000,
         cassava_pc_2024 = (cassava_Area_2024/pop_est_2025) * 10000, 
         cowpea_pc_2024 = (cowpea_Area_2024/pop_est_2025) * 10000, 
         maize_pc_2024 = (maize_Area_2024/pop_est_2025) * 10000, 
         rice_pc_2024 = (rice_Area_2024/pop_est_2025) * 10000, 
         sorghum_pc_2024 = (sorghum_Area_2024/pop_est_2025) * 10000, 
         spot_pc_2020 = (spot_Area_2020/pop_est_2025) * 10000)

vect_crop_area_pc <- dplyr::left_join(vect_state_geo, df_crop_per_capita_2024_pc , by = c("adm1_ref_name"))

```

# Crop area per state as proportion of national total

## Plantain/Banana national area share

```{r}
#| label: plantain_banana_state_area_share
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: false
#| results: asis
#| 

plantain_banana_area_2024_total <-  
  df_plantain_banana_2024_rename |>
  dplyr::summarise(total = sum(plantain_banana_Area_2024, na.rm=T)) |> pull(total)

df_plantain_banana_2024_national_share <- df_plantain_banana_2024_rename |> 
  mutate(plantain_banana_Area_2024_pc = (plantain_banana_Area_2024 / plantain_banana_area_2024_total)) 

df_plantain_banana_2024_national_share[is.na(df_plantain_banana_2024_national_share)] <- 0

write.csv(df_plantain_banana_2024_national_share, "tab_data/plantain_banana_area_national_share.csv")

```
